stem: A developer's loop runs `get_customer`, then sends the output back as `{"role": "tool", "content": "..."}`. The API rejects the request. What is the correct way to return the result?

options.text: Add a `session_id` so the API can match the result to the earlier call
options.explanation: The API has no session parameter; each call is stateless and matching is done by `tool_use_id` inside the message.

options.text: Send it as an `assistant` message, since the assistant asked for the tool
options.explanation: The assistant turn holds the `tool_use` request; the result must come from the user side.

options.text: Send a `user` message containing a `tool_result` block whose `tool_use_id` matches the request
options.explanation: Correct: there is no tool role; results go in a user-role `tool_result` block linked by `tool_use_id`.

options.text: Put the tool output into the `system` field for the next call
options.explanation: The system prompt is for instructions, not for tool results; the pairing with the `tool_use` block would be lost.

keyPrinciple: Tool results travel as `tool_result` blocks in a user message, linked by `tool_use_id`.

stem: An agent often stops right after saying "Let me check your order status." The loop exits as soon as a response contains any text block. What should the exit condition be?

options.text: Exit only when `stop_reason` is `"end_turn"`
options.explanation: Correct: that response also held a `tool_use` block; only `stop_reason` reliably says the task is finished.

options.text: Tell the model to write DONE when finished, and exit when the text contains DONE
options.explanation: Parsing natural language has no contract; the model may phrase it differently or say it early.

options.text: Exit after a fixed number of iterations, e.g. five
options.explanation: A cap stops long tasks too early and doesn't detect completion; at most it is a safety net.

options.text: Exit when `stop_reason` is `"max_tokens"` or the response has text
options.explanation: `max_tokens` means the output was cut off, not that the task is complete.

keyPrinciple: Only `stop_reason == "end_turn"` ends the loop; text content is not a completion signal.

stem: A coordinator's prompt says "delegate each subtopic to the search agent", but logs show it never spawns anything and writes the answers itself. Its config is `allowed_tools=["summarize"]`. Most likely cause?

options.text: The prompt needs stronger wording, such as "you MUST delegate"
options.explanation: No wording helps when the coordinator has no tool for spawning subagents at all.

options.text: The search agent's description is too short for the coordinator to find it
options.explanation: Description quality matters for choosing among subagents, but the coordinator can't invoke any of them yet.

options.text: Subagents need shared memory with the coordinator before they can start
options.explanation: Subagents have isolated context by design; shared memory isn't how spawning works.

options.text: `"Task"` is missing from the coordinator's allowed tools
options.explanation: Correct: subagents are spawned through the Task tool, so without it delegation is impossible.

keyPrinciple: A coordinator can only spawn subagents if `Task` is in its allowed tools.

stem: A research coordinator spawns three independent subagents, one per turn, and each takes about 40 seconds. How do you cut total latency without changing the subagents?

options.text: Merge the three subagents into one agent with all their tools
options.explanation: That changes the architecture and gives one agent too many tools; it also does the work in sequence.

options.text: Have the coordinator emit all three `Task` calls in one response
options.explanation: Correct: multiple Task calls in one response run in parallel.

options.text: Switch the subagent calls to the Message Batches API
options.explanation: Batches trade latency for cost and can take up to 24 hours; it makes this slower, not faster.

options.text: Lower `max_tokens` so each subagent finishes sooner
options.explanation: It may truncate results and doesn't remove the one-after-another pattern that causes the delay.

keyPrinciple: Parallel subagents = several `Task` calls in one coordinator response.

stem: On Monday you investigated a billing module in the named session `billing-bug`. On Tuesday a teammate changed 2 of the 14 files it read. What is the best way to continue?

options.text: Start a new session and re-explore all 14 files
options.explanation: Most of the earlier findings are still valid; re-exploring everything wastes them.

options.text: Use `fork_session` so the original session stays untouched
options.explanation: Forking is for trying divergent approaches; it still carries the same stale results for the 2 files.

options.text: Resume `billing-bug` and tell it which 2 files changed
options.explanation: Correct: most context is still valid, and naming the changed files triggers a targeted re-check.

options.text: Resume `billing-bug` without comment; it will notice the changes
options.explanation: Resume does not check file state; the agent may trust its old reads of the changed files.

keyPrinciple: Resume when context is mostly valid, and name the files that changed.

stem: Downstream code always parses an `extract_invoice` tool call. About 3% of responses are plain prose ("Here is the invoice data: ..."), and the parser crashes. The request uses `tool_choice: {"type": "auto"}`. Best fix?

options.text: Add "always respond with a tool call" to the system prompt
options.explanation: Still probabilistic; the prose replies become rarer but don't disappear.

options.text: Retry any prose response with the same request
options.explanation: With `auto` the same request can produce prose again; it treats the symptom.

options.text: Raise `max_tokens` so the model has room to call the tool
options.explanation: The prose replies are complete, not truncated; token room isn't the problem.

options.text: Set `tool_choice` to `{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"}`
options.explanation: Correct: forcing the tool guarantees a tool call, so the parser always gets structured input.

keyPrinciple: When code needs a tool call every time, don't use `auto`; force it.

stem: A product-sheet schema has `"warranty_months": {"type": "integer"}` in `required`. Many sheets don't mention a warranty, yet the output often says `12`. What should change?

options.text: Make it `["integer", "null"]` and describe `null` as "not stated in the document"
options.explanation: Correct: a required non-null field forces a value; nullable gives an honest option for missing data.

options.text: Add "do not guess the warranty" to the prompt and keep the field required
options.explanation: The schema still demands an integer, so the pressure to invent one remains.

options.text: Replace it with an enum of common warranty lengths
options.explanation: An enum still forces a pick when nothing is stated; it doesn't allow absence.

options.text: Retry the extraction until a warranty is found
options.explanation: Retrying can't find information the document never contained.

keyPrinciple: Fields that may be absent from the source must be nullable, or the model will invent values.

stem: An MCP tool `search_orders` returns `[]` both when the database is unreachable and when a customer has no orders. During an outage, the agent tells customers they have no orders. Best fix?

options.text: Return the string "Operation failed" whenever the result is empty
options.explanation: Real empty results would now look like failures, and the message gives no category or retry guidance.

options.text: Tell the agent to retry three times whenever it gets an empty list
options.explanation: It wastes calls on genuine empty results and still can't tell the two cases apart.

options.text: On failure, return `isError: true` with a transient category and `isRetryable: true`; on no matches, return an empty result without an error
options.explanation: Correct: the agent can now tell "could not look" from "looked and found nothing".

options.text: Return `null` in both cases so the agent treats them with caution
options.explanation: Same problem in a new shape: the two situations still look identical.

keyPrinciple: An access failure and a valid empty result must look different to the agent.

stem: A synthesis agent gets Q3 churn figures from two credible internal sources: a finance dashboard says 4.1% and a CRM export says 5.3%. What should the final output contain?

options.text: The average, 4.7%, with both sources cited
options.explanation: Averaging creates a number neither source reported and hides that they differ.

options.text: Both values with their sources and a conflict flag
options.explanation: Correct: same period, different values is a real conflict; keep both with attribution and flag it for the coordinator.

options.text: Only the finance dashboard figure, as the more official source
options.explanation: Picking one silently drops evidence a reviewer would need.

options.text: Leave out churn until the sources agree
options.explanation: It drops useful information instead of reporting it with its uncertainty.

keyPrinciple: Conflicting sources for the same period: keep both, attributed, and flag the conflict.

stem: A Message Batch of 2,000 contracts finishes. 37 requests failed because the documents were too long. The other results are fine. What next?

options.text: Find the 37 by `custom_id`, split those documents into chunks, and resubmit only them
options.explanation: Correct: `custom_id` lets you fix and resend just the failed items.

options.text: Resubmit the whole batch with a higher `max_tokens`
options.explanation: It redoes 1,963 good results, and `max_tokens` limits output, not input length.

options.text: Move the whole job to the synchronous API
options.explanation: Doubles the cost and doesn't fix the oversized inputs.

options.text: Rewrite the prompt and run a new sample before anything else
options.explanation: The prompt works for most documents; this is an input-size problem in a few items.

keyPrinciple: Isolated batch failures: fix and resubmit only those items via `custom_id`.

stem: A senior developer wrote "use pnpm, never npm" in their `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Claude follows it for them, but new hires' sessions keep using npm. Best fix?

options.text: Add a step to the onboarding doc asking everyone to copy the line into their own file
options.explanation: Manual copying drifts and gets forgotten; it treats a scope problem as a communication problem.

options.text: Import `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` into the project CLAUDE.md with `@`
options.explanation: That path points to each developer's own home folder, which doesn't contain the senior's rule.

options.text: Move the line into the project's committed CLAUDE.md
options.explanation: Correct: the project file is shared through version control, so every session gets it.

options.text: Create a `/use-pnpm` command that new hires run each session
options.explanation: Commands load only when invoked; people will forget, and it should apply always.

keyPrinciple: Team-wide, always-on rules go in the project CLAUDE.md, not user-level files.

stem: A team adds `.claude/rules/sql.md` with migration conventions and no frontmatter. They expected it to apply only to `.sql` files. What actually happens, and what is the fix?

options.text: It never loads; rules need an `enabled: true` key
options.explanation: There is no such key; a rules file without frontmatter loads.

options.text: It loads in every session; add `paths: ["**/*.sql"]` frontmatter
options.explanation: Correct: without `paths:` a rules file is always loaded, like CLAUDE.md.

options.text: It loads only for `.sql` files, because the file name is `sql.md`
options.explanation: There is no scoping by file name; only the `paths:` glob makes a rule conditional.

options.text: It loads only when someone runs `/sql`
options.explanation: That describes commands or skills, not rules files.

keyPrinciple: Only `paths:` frontmatter makes a rules file conditional.

stem: `.claude/rules/terraform.md` has `paths: ["**/*.tf"]`. `.claude/rules/infra.md` has `paths: ["infra/**/*"]`. Claude edits `infra/web/main.tf`. Which rules load?

options.text: Only `terraform.md`, because it is more specific
options.explanation: There is no specificity ranking between rules files.

options.text: Only `infra.md`, because its folder pattern comes first
options.explanation: Pattern order doesn't pick a winner; every matching rule applies.

options.text: Neither, because two matches conflict
options.explanation: Overlapping matches aren't an error; both simply load.

options.text: Both, because the file matches both globs
options.explanation: Correct: loading depends only on whether a glob matches, so both rules load.

keyPrinciple: Every rules file whose `paths:` glob matches loads; there is no priority.

stem: Security requires that Claude Code can never run `git push --force` in this repository, with no exceptions. Which option actually guarantees it?

options.text: A hook (or a settings deny rule) that blocks the command before it runs
options.explanation: Correct: it runs as code before the command, whatever the model decides. If you use a deny rule, keep the pattern broad, since narrow argument patterns can be bypassed.

options.text: "NEVER force push" in capital letters in the project CLAUDE.md
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md is context; the model usually follows it, but there is no guarantee.

options.text: A rules file with `paths: [".git/**"]` that forbids force pushes
options.explanation: Rules are also context, and a push doesn't mean editing files under `.git/`.

options.text: A skill that explains safe git workflows
options.explanation: A skill only loads when invoked and is still just guidance.

keyPrinciple: Zero-exception rules need enforcement (hooks, deny rules), not context files.
sourceRef: Exam Guide TS 1.4, 1.5; permission rules: Claude Code docs (settings)

stem: You want to try an experimental database MCP server for a week without affecting teammates. Where do you configure it?

options.text: In `.mcp.json`, using `${VAR}` for the connection string
options.explanation: `.mcp.json` is committed and shared, so every teammate would get the server.

options.text: In `~/.claude.json`
options.explanation: Correct: user scope is for personal and experimental servers and isn't shared.

options.text: In `.claude/rules/mcp.md`
options.explanation: Rules files hold instructions; they don't configure MCP servers.

options.text: In `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` as a server list
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md is instructions, not server configuration.

keyPrinciple: Team MCP servers → `.mcp.json`; personal or experimental → `~/.claude.json`.

stem: CI runs `claude -p "Review this PR" --output-format json`. The comment poster sometimes crashes because the JSON has no `findings` array. What should you add?

options.text: `--strict`, so the output format is enforced
options.explanation: No such flag exists; the output shape needs a schema.

options.text: A sentence in the prompt: "always include a findings array"
options.explanation: Prompt wording makes it more likely, not guaranteed.

options.text: `--json-schema` with a schema that requires `findings`
options.explanation: Correct: the schema makes the JSON match the shape the poster expects.

options.text: Switch to text output and extract findings with a regex
options.explanation: That goes back to parsing free text, which is less reliable than what you have now.

keyPrinciple: `--output-format json` gives JSON; `--json-schema` gives the right shape.

stem: A pull request adds `.claude/config.json` containing `{"commands": ["deploy-check"]}` and a prompt file. After merging, `/deploy-check` isn't available. Why?

options.text: Claude Code needs a restart to read the new config file
options.explanation: A restart won't help; Claude Code doesn't read this file for commands at all.

options.text: The entry also needs `"enabled": true`
options.explanation: The key is invented, like the file; nothing reads it.

options.text: The file must be in `~/.claude/config.json`
options.explanation: That location is invented too.

options.text: That file isn't a Claude Code mechanism; the command must be `.claude/commands/deploy-check.md`
options.explanation: Correct: each command is its own Markdown file in the commands folder.

keyPrinciple: Commands are files in `.claude/commands/`; `.claude/config.json` is an exam distractor.

stem: Before a refactor, you need to know how a 200-file legacy module is wired together. You only need a short summary in your main session. What is the best first move?

options.text: Delegate the discovery to the Explore subagent and keep its summary
options.explanation: Correct: the verbose reads stay in the subagent, and the main context keeps only the result.

options.text: Read all 200 files in the main session, then run `/compact`
options.explanation: It fills the context first and then loses detail in a summary; avoiding the bloat is better.

options.text: Run `/memory` to load the module into context
options.explanation: `/memory` shows and edits memory files; it doesn't explore code.

options.text: Run `/compact` now, before exploring
options.explanation: There is nothing to compact yet; it doesn't keep the future discovery output out of context.

keyPrinciple: Keep verbose discovery out of the main context with the Explore subagent.

stem: Documents arrive all day, and each must be processed within 30 hours of arrival. You use the Message Batches API (up to 24 hours per batch). How often should you submit batches?

options.text: Once a day, with everything that arrived
options.explanation: A document can wait up to 24 h for the daily batch, then take 24 h more: 48 h, far past the SLA.

options.text: Every 12 hours
options.explanation: 12 h wait + 24 h processing = 36 h worst case, which breaks the 30 h SLA.

options.text: Every 4 hours
options.explanation: Correct: at most 4 h waiting + 24 h processing = 28 h, inside 30 h with margin (the exam guide's own example).

options.text: Whenever convenient, since batches usually finish much faster
options.explanation: There is no latency SLA; you must plan for the full 24 hours.

keyPrinciple: Submission window + 24 h worst-case processing must fit inside the SLA.

stem: A nightly job writes 5,000 product descriptions. A product manager reviews them the next morning. The job uses the synchronous API and costs too much. Most effective change?

options.text: Run the synchronous calls in parallel to finish faster
options.explanation: Speed isn't the goal here; the cost stays the same.

options.text: Submit the job through the Message Batches API
options.explanation: Correct: nobody waits overnight, so 50% cheaper with up to 24 h processing fits.

options.text: Batch with a fallback to synchronous calls if it's slow
options.explanation: Over-engineered: there is no latency requirement to protect.

options.text: Lower `max_tokens` to shorten each description
options.explanation: It changes the output quality instead of the pricing model that fits this workload.

keyPrinciple: "Overnight" and "nobody is waiting" in the stem point to the Batches API.

stem: An agent sometimes sends a price quote to a customer before a manager's approval is recorded. The system prompt already says "only send quotes after approval". Best fix?

options.text: Add few-shot examples that show waiting for approval
options.explanation: Still prompt-based; the failure rate drops but isn't zero.

options.text: Ask the agent to double-check approval before every send
options.explanation: A self-check runs in the same reasoning that made the mistake; no guarantee.

options.text: Block the `send_quote` call in code until an approval record exists
options.explanation: Correct: a prerequisite gate or hook makes skipping the approval impossible.

options.text: Move the rule into CLAUDE.md and mark it IMPORTANT
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md is still context the model may not follow.

keyPrinciple: A required order of actions needs a code-level gate, not better wording.

stem: An agent writes API docs and then reviews them in the same session with "now critically check your work". Wrong parameter names still reach production. Best change?

options.text: Turn on extended thinking for the review step
options.explanation: More reasoning, but in the same context that produced the errors.

options.text: Run the review twice in the same session
options.explanation: Repeats the same bias; the session keeps defending its own choices.

options.text: Make the review instruction stricter and longer
options.explanation: The problem is the shared context, not the wording of the instruction.

options.text: Review with a separate instance that didn't write the docs
options.explanation: Correct: an independent instance has none of the generation reasoning.

keyPrinciple: Self-review can't escape its own reasoning; use an independent instance.

stem: A support agent escalates whenever message sentiment is strongly negative. Escalations are high, yet calm customers with policy exceptions get wrong answers. Best redesign?

options.text: Tune the sentiment threshold with a few weeks of data
options.explanation: A better-tuned proxy is still a proxy; mood doesn't show case complexity.

options.text: Escalate on an explicit request for a human, a policy gap, or no progress after several attempts
options.explanation: Correct: these triggers are based on the facts of the request, not mood.

options.text: Escalate when the model's self-reported confidence is below 0.7
options.explanation: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, especially on the hard cases.

options.text: Escalate every conversation longer than ten messages
options.explanation: Length isn't complexity; it escalates chatty easy cases and misses short policy gaps.

keyPrinciple: Escalation triggers: explicit request, policy gap, no progress; not sentiment or self-confidence.

stem: A review of a 60-file pull request catches bugs in the first and last files but misses obvious ones in the middle. What fix fits best?

options.text: Per-file review passes, plus a separate pass for cross-file issues
options.explanation: Correct: each file gets full attention, and the integration pass catches issues between files.

options.text: Use a model with a larger context window
options.explanation: Capacity isn't the problem; attention across a long input stays uneven.

options.text: Add "review every file with equal care" to the prompt
options.explanation: An instruction doesn't change how attention spreads across a long input.

options.text: Put the 60 files in alphabetical order
options.explanation: Reordering only moves which files land in the middle.

keyPrinciple: Attention dilution is fixed by splitting passes, not by a bigger window.

stem: A market report on electric vehicles should cover the whole industry. The coordinator assigned "battery costs" and "Tesla sales". Each subagent did excellent work, but the report misses charging networks and policy. Where is the fix?

options.text: Tell the synthesis agent to find and fill coverage gaps
options.explanation: Synthesis can only combine what it received; this blames a spoke for a hub problem.

options.text: Give the search subagents broader, more general queries
options.explanation: They did what they were assigned; the assignments were the problem.

options.text: Broaden the coordinator's task decomposition to cover all subtopics
options.explanation: Correct: the gap was created when the topic was split into too few subtasks.

options.text: Add a second report-generation agent to review completeness
options.explanation: Over-engineered and still downstream of the real cause.

keyPrinciple: Good subagent work + narrow coverage = a decomposition problem at the coordinator.

stem: A document-analysis subagent can't parse 1 of 40 PDFs because the file is corrupted. What should it send back to the coordinator?

options.text: Results for 39 documents, reported as a full success
options.explanation: It hides the gap; the final report would seem complete when it isn't.

options.text: An error that stops the whole research run
options.explanation: Overreacts: 39 good results would be lost because of one file.

options.text: Results for 39, plus a structured error: which file, failure type, and possible alternatives
options.explanation: Correct: the coordinator keeps the good work and can decide what to do about the missing file.

options.text: Nothing yet; keep retrying the corrupted file until it parses
options.explanation: A corrupted file won't parse on retry; it just blocks everything.

keyPrinciple: Report failures with structure and partial results; don't hide them or stop everything.

stem: The team wants an on-demand `/codebase-report` workflow. It produces pages of verbose analysis that shouldn't clutter the main session, and it must not be able to run destructive commands. What fits best?

options.text: A slash command file in `.claude/commands/`
options.explanation: The exam guide ties isolation (`context: fork`) and tool restriction (`allowed-tools`) to skills; a plain command is the weaker answer here.

options.text: A project skill with `context: fork` and `allowed-tools` limited to read and file-write tools
options.explanation: Correct: fork isolates the verbose output, and allowed-tools keeps destructive tools out.

options.text: A section in the project CLAUDE.md describing the steps
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md is always-loaded context, not an invokable workflow.

options.text: A rules file with `paths: ["src/**/*"]`
options.explanation: Rules load when editing matching files; they aren't invoked on demand and give no isolation or tool limits.

keyPrinciple: Need isolation or tool limits for an on-demand workflow → skill, not command.

stem: Three MCP tools return dates as a Unix timestamp, "Mar 5, 2025" and ISO 8601. The agent sometimes compares them wrongly. Where do you fix this?

options.text: A `PreToolUse` hook that reformats the tools' input arguments
options.explanation: The inputs aren't the problem; the mixed formats come back in the results.

options.text: A system prompt that explains all three formats
options.explanation: The model still converts each date itself, so errors stay possible.

options.text: Force `tool_choice` so the tools are called in a fixed order
options.explanation: The order of calls doesn't change the formats returned.

options.text: A `PostToolUse` hook that converts every result to ISO 8601
options.explanation: Correct: it changes results after the tool runs and before Claude sees them, the same way every time.

keyPrinciple: Normalise tool results with PostToolUse; block or redirect calls with PreToolUse.

stem: Early on, a customer said "I was charged $149.50 twice on March 3." After 30 turns of summarised history, the agent talks about "a charge of about $150 in March". Best fix?

options.text: Keep a case-facts block with the exact amount, date and request in every prompt
options.explanation: Correct: the facts stay outside the summary, so they don't lose precision.

options.text: Run `/compact` more often
options.explanation: Compacting is summarising; it would blur the details even more.

options.text: Switch to a model with a larger context window
options.explanation: The details were lost in summarisation, not because of a size limit.

options.text: Ask the customer to repeat the details before any refund
options.explanation: It shifts the burden to the customer and doesn't stop the drift.

keyPrinciple: Exact numbers, IDs and dates belong in a persistent case-facts block, not in summaries.

stem: A schema has `notice_period: {"enum": ["30_days", "60_days", "90_days", "unclear", "other"]}` plus a nullable `notice_detail`. A contract clearly says "45 days". What should the output be?

options.text: `"60_days"`, the nearest listed value
options.explanation: Rounding to a listed value turns a clear fact into a wrong one.

options.text: `"unclear"`, since 45 isn't a listed option
options.explanation: The contract is clear; "unclear" is for ambiguous source text.

options.text: `"other"` with `notice_detail: "45 days"`
options.explanation: Correct: a clear value outside the list goes to "other" plus detail.

options.text: `null`, since no listed value fits
options.explanation: `null` means the information is missing; here it is present.

keyPrinciple: Absent → null; ambiguous → "unclear"; clear but not listed → "other" + detail.

stem: Claude's new pagination code has two bugs: the page-size default is wrong, and the cursor encoding breaks when the page size changes. How should you report them?

options.text: Fix the page-size default first, then report the cursor bug in a later message
options.explanation: The fixes interact: changing the page size affects the cursor, so fixing one alone may break or hide the other.

options.text: Describe both in one detailed message, because the fixes affect each other
options.explanation: Correct: interacting issues belong in one message so both fixes are designed together.

options.text: Re-describe the whole pagination requirement in different words
options.explanation: Rephrasing the requirement gives no stable target; point to the specific failures instead.

options.text: Report whichever bug is more severe and ignore the other until later
options.explanation: Leaving an interacting bug for later risks a fix that has to be redone.

keyPrinciple: Interacting issues → one message; independent issues → fix one at a time.

stem: A customer writes: "This is the second broken blender! Ridiculous." The replacement policy clearly covers this case. What should the agent do first?

options.text: Escalate to a human, since the customer is clearly upset
options.explanation: Frustration alone isn't a trigger; the issue is solvable and the customer hasn't asked for a human.

options.text: Ask the customer whether they would like to speak to a human
options.explanation: It skips the resolution the agent can already offer and nudges toward an unneeded escalation.

options.text: Process a replacement right away without replying to the complaint
options.explanation: Resolving is right, but ignoring the frustration misses the acknowledgement step the guide describes.

options.text: Acknowledge the frustration and offer a replacement; escalate only if they then insist on a human
options.explanation: Correct: solvable issue → acknowledge and offer resolution; escalate if the customer repeats their preference.

keyPrinciple: Frustrated but solvable: acknowledge, offer the fix, escalate only if the customer asks again.
